newsitem.title: USA: Prosecution rests in Arizona governor's trial.
newsitem.headline: Prosecution rests in Arizona governor's trial.

text.p: Prosecutors rested their case against embattled Arizona Gov. Fife Symington on Thursday with an emotional portrayal of him as a man who refused to listen to his top company executive and treated her badly.
Jean Wong, former executive vice president of The Symington Co., said she quit her job because she no longer was being consulted on decisions being made by the Republican politician.
"I faced the realisation that not even I could change or control Fife," she told the jury in the federal fraud trial.
With tears in her eyes, Wong concluded by saying she would never again do business with her former boss "because I can't believe the way he treated me after I left the company."
Defence attorneys contended during cross-examination that Wong was a disgruntled employee, who got all the benefits of the job without the risk faced by Symington.
The defence began arguing its case later on Thursday.

Symington faces 22 felony charges including fraud, extortion and perjury. If convicted on even a single count, the two-term governor would be ousted from the office he has held since 1991. He also faces a possible prison term.
Prosecutors concluded their case with two days of testimony from Wong, who described her former boss as a risk-taker who knew his way around a calculator.
Her remarks countered defence claims that Symington concerned himself with the larger picture, and that he was neither hands-on nor detail-oriented.
Federal prosecutors claim Symington knew what he was doing when he submitted "blatently false" financial statements to various lenders to keep his real estate empire from collapsing.

The government has spent 10 weeks painstakingly taking the eight-man, eight-woman jury through reams of financial documents covering Symington's personal and business transactions from the mid-1980s to the early 1990s.
During the trial, the government presented evidence that Symington reported a fat bottom line to lenders he was courting and a negative net worth to those who were pressing him for payment of debts.
Several lenders said they relied on the statements when making loan decisions and would not have given Symington the money he sought if they had been made aware of his true financial picture.

Prosecutors also spent the last several days outlining allegations that the governor used his office in an attempt to extort concessions from unions who loaned him $10 million to finance a Phoenix shopping centre.

A former union pension fund adviser alleged Symington threatened to use his influence to scuttle a major lease at the centre unless he was released from his personal guarantee and mortgage payments were changed.
Defence attorneys maintain there was no extortion, and that the adviser had a personal vendetta against Symington.

The prosecution also used Symington's own voice -- recorded at a bankruptcy hearing -- in an attempt to prove that he committed perjury in statements made to creditors. He filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy protection in September 1995.
Defence attorney John Dowd acknowledged that mistakes were made, but that the errors were not intentional and did not affect decisions made by various lenders.
He is expected to take the next several weeks presenting his case. Dowd told reporters that he still has not yet decided whether Symington will testify.
The jury is slated to begin deliberations in mid-August
